info.headline: Say one clear sentence: short, framed spoken responses about familiar topics.
info.summary: Level A speakers produce short, complete spoken sentences about familiar school and personal topics, leaning heavily on sentence frames, word banks, and visual supports. Tasks center on naming, describing what they see, stating a simple opinion with a reason, and retelling in order. Success means one clear idea spoken in a complete sentence, often rehearsed before delivery.
info.distinguishes: Level A responses are 1–2 short sentences built directly from a provided frame, using everyday and high-frequency academic words and concrete, picture-supported prompts. Speakers rely on frames and choral rehearsal and are not yet expected to connect multiple ideas, add transitions, or justify with evidence — that independence and extended, cohesive discourse is the Level B step up.

I can use polite social phrases to greet, introduce, and ask for help.
I can compare two familiar pictures using same and different.

info.summary: Level C speakers give extended, well-organized responses on academic topics. models.B: Pitcher B is stronger. To compare, I used the same amount of water for both. If I use 15 cups of water, Pitcher A needs 9 cups of juice and Pitcher B needs 10 cups of juice. Ten is more than nine, so Pitcher B has more lemon juice for the same water. That means B tastes stronger.

activities.title: Summarize a Short Story: The Broken Bridge
activities.skill: Summarizing the main events of a story in your own words

He realized that a problem feels smaller when many people share the work. Summarize this story.

activities.title: Explain a Theme: What Does Mina's Story Teach?
activities.skill: Explaining how text details support a theme
activities.directions: Read the short story. Then speak 6-8 sentences: state the theme as a full sentence, give two details from the story as evidence, and explain how each detail shows the theme.
activities.prompt: Story: Mina practiced the violin every day, but at her first concert she played the wrong notes and froze. Embarrassed, she wanted to quit. Her teacher said, "Every musician has a bad night." Mina went home, practiced slowly, and signed up for the spring concert. At that concert, she made another mistake, but this time she kept playing until the last note. What is the theme, and which details prove it?
activities.responsePlaceholder: Theme (a full sentence): ___ / Detail 1: ___ / Detail 2: ___ / How they show the theme: ___

models.A: The theme is do not quit. Mina made a mistake. She practiced again. She played at the next concert.
models.B: The theme of this story is that you should keep trying after you fail. At first, Mina froze and wanted to quit. Then she practiced slowly and signed up for the spring concert. This shows that she did not give up. Because of that, the author teaches us to keep trying.
models.C: The theme of this story is that failure is not the end; it is a chance to grow if you keep trying. The author supports this idea with two key details. However, she went home, practiced slowly, and signed up for the spring concert, which proves that she chose perseverance over embarrassment. Second, at the spring concert she made another mistake but kept playing until the last note. This detail shows that she had changed. Therefore, the author suggests that courage means continuing after you stumble.
